body.text: Marrying outside one’s religion or caste has never been easy in India, where centuries of caste and community endogamy have left a measurable imprint on the country’s genetic structure. It’s only gotten tougher in the past decade, as Hindu nationalist governments in state after state enacted laws to restrict or regulate interfaith marriages in different ways.

A couple in the western Indian state of Maharashtra is among the latest victims. In October, Shravani Rane, 22, and Faiz Akbar Khan, 26, registered their marriage under the Special Marriage Act, 1954, which governs marriage without involving religion or religious conversion. Yet, Rane’s mother filed a police complaint against Khan under the new Maharashtra Freedom of Religion Act, 2026, for unlawful conversion by “allurement or marriage-related deception.”

The act came into force on August 28, 2026. Section 3 prohibits conversion through allurement, coercion, deceit, force, misrepresentation, threats, undue influence and fraudulent means, including marriage or relationship. Section 8(1) allows the converted person’s parents, siblings and other specified relatives to lodge a police complaint.

Both Rane and Khan told the media their marriage does not involve religious conversion, but they are facing harassment nonetheless, with Khan having to appear before the police several times. On November 16, Rane rebutted the family’s charges in a court in the presence of her family members.

This incident happened at a time when the government in the eastern state of West Bengal – which Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) won in May 2026 – expressed its intention to regulate inter-faith marriages. The government will enact a law to prevent “love jihad,” the state’s chief minister Suvendu Adhikari said in October.

“Love Jihad” is a Hindu nationalist conspiracy theory alleging that Muslim men systematically lure Hindu women into romantic relationships and marriages to convert them to Islam, as part of a purported demographic or religious campaign.
This has earned wide popularity since the Hindu nationalist BJP came to power in India in 2014.

At least 13 Indian states have laws regulating religious conversion, according to the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom. Some of these laws date back several decades. However, a new wave of legislation and amendments has appeared since 2017 – in Jharkhand (2017), Uttarakhand (2018), Himachal Pradesh (2019), Uttar Pradesh (2021), Madhya Pradesh (2021), Karnataka (2022), Haryana (2022), Rajasthan (2025), Maharashtra (2026) and Chhattisgarh (2026).
They have expanded restrictions, including provisions that specifically target conversions allegedly undertaken through marriage. These laws have come to be popularly described as “love jihad laws.”

Whether the marriage involves religious conversion or not, the heat is coming on all sorts of interfaith couples intending to marry. This is particularly because vigilantes are using a provision in the Special Marriage Act as a loophole to thwart such marriages.

The law requires the couple to serve notice to the marriage officer 30 days before the date of marriage. This notice must be displayed at the marriage registrar’s office for people to raise objections. This helps prevent fraudulent marriages, including underage, prohibited kinships or existing marriages, it has been argued.

However, in recent years, vigilantes have kept their eyes on notice boards at marriage registrars’ offices. Vigilante groups have tracked notices submitted by interfaith couples, circulated them on social media and sometimes brought them to the attention of their families, exposing couples to harassment and threats.
A recent report by the independent news outlet Article 14 revealed a strikingly increasing gap between couples serving notice of marriage to the registrar and ultimately not registering the marriage.

It showed that, between 2013 and 2015, Delhi recorded 1,636 applications under the Special Marriage Act and 1,634 registrations – a gap of only two. This figure dipped to only 214 registrations against 1,026 applications in 2024 and 153 registrations against 1,053 notices in 2025.

The two sets of figures are not cohort-linked. A December application may be registered in January. Some couples may willingly postpone their marriage. Nevertheless, the comparison reveals a dramatic widening gap between marriage notices and registrations.

In 2013-15, registrations almost matched applications. The proportion of registrations out of applications slid to 82.34 percent in 2016-2018, 76.88 percent between October 2019 and February 2023, and 45.66 percent between March and December 2023. In 2024 and 2025, the share stood at only 20.86 percent and 14.53 percent, respectively.

Author Ismat Ara documented many incidents of interfaith relationships with tragic consequences, especially involving Muslim men and Hindu women, in her recent book, “Under a Saffron Sky: Inside India’s Crackdown on Love.” She pointed out that less than 3 percent of marriages in India are actually interfaith, revealing how this has never been an easy choice. The politicization of faith and choice has now made it much more difficult.

In a September 2026 interview with The Diplomat’s South Asia editor, Sudha Ramachandran, Ara said vigilantism involves many forms of mobilization, including surveillance, family pressure, public intervention, ideological programming, and street action. Together, they create an environment in which the wider community feels entitled to police interfaith relationships.
“Once people believe the myth of ‘love jihad,’ real couples have to live with its consequences,” Ara said.

In March 2018, the Supreme Court delivered two landmark judgments that should have protected these couples. In Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M., the top court affirmed that the right to marry a person of one’s choice is integral to Article 21 of the Constitution. Matters of love, partnership, and faith fall within the protected sphere of personal identity, and neither the State nor society can intrude on an individual’s choice of partner.

In Shakti Vahini v. Union of India, the apex court laid down preventive, remedial and punitive measures to protect couples against honor-based violence. The Court held that family or community consent is unnecessary when two adults decide to marry, and that families or communities cannot interfere with their marriages.

Yet, the provisions of the new anti-conversion laws work in the opposite direction. Several state anti-conversion laws require advance declarations or prior permission for religious conversion, often accompanied by disclosure of family details.

In Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, the prescribed declarations require parents’ names and addresses; Gujarat and Haryana also collect family-identifying information. Maharashtra’s 2026 law goes further: it requires 60 days’ advance notice, public display of proposed conversion notices and a post-conversion declaration containing the parents’ names and addresses. Some of these laws also permit or require police inquiries into the intention and circumstances of the proposed conversion.

A deadly combination of the public disclosure requirements under the Special Marriage Act, the growing reach of anti-conversion legislation and politically motivated vigilantism seems to have created an environment in which consenting adults’ most intimate choices can become matters of official scrutiny and family or community intervention. They threaten to expose couples to precisely the kind of hostility and interference against which the Supreme Court sought to protect them in 2018.
